attributes.description: Fires when PostgREST records database pool timeouts. Every increment is an API request that gave up waiting for a database connection, so this is a user-visible failure and the highest-signal PostgREST error metric.
attributes.name: [Supabase OTel] PostgREST database pool timeouts

investigation_guide.blob:
## PostgREST Database Pool Timeouts

PostgREST holds its own connection pool. A timeout means an incoming REST request waited for a database connection and never got one, so the caller received an error. This is user-visible.

### Triage Steps
1. Read the `Pool Waiting` column: a non-zero value confirms requests are queueing for connections rather than failing for another reason.
2. Treat this as a symptom, not a cause. Work up the chain: disk IO utilisation, then mean query time from `pg_stat_statements_total_time_seconds / pg_stat_statements_total_queries`, then long-running transactions, and only then pool sizing.
3. Check whether the whole Postgres connection budget is exhausted — if it is, PostgREST cannot grow its pool no matter how it is configured.
4. `pgrst_db_pool_available` versus `pgrst_db_pool_max` is easily misread: the pool is established lazily, so a low `available` at idle is normal. Trust `waiting` and `timeouts` instead.

### Tuning
Any timeout is actionable, so the threshold is greater than zero. Raise it if your clients retry transparently and you only care about sustained failure.

### Related content
The absence of pool timeouts over a rolling window is tracked as an SLO. This rule targets the acute occurrence.
